title: UK bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF
content: Bluefin tuna have returned in huge numbers off the British coast after almost disappearing from UK waters. The return of the giant predatory fish is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF, which it says shows conservation can work. However, the Living Planet Report 2026 also found that monitored wildlife populations around the world have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970. The wildlife conservation charity said nature remains in "freefall" but it called the report one of hope. "It's not too late," Mike Barrett, chief scientific adviser at WWF-UK, told the BBC. The UK was once home to large tuna fisheries, but overfishing of both the tuna and the smaller fish it preys on meant that by the 1960s it had largely disappeared. The report credits its recent recovery to a concerted international effort that included reducing catch quotas, size limits and protection of spawning grounds, which was backed by campaigns from consumers, chefs and retailers. Hannah Rudd, head of marine at the Angling Trust, said the result of this effort was close to an "explosion" in the population of the species. "I think bluefin tuna is a golden case study that fisheries management works," she said. The WWF report highlighted other species recoveries around the world, including an increase of more than 70% in the number of wild tigers - from around 3,200 in 2010 to about 5,700 in 2025. Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to have its protection status downgraded from "endangered" to "least concern", after 50 years of conservation work in about 80 countries. Elephant numbers are stable or growing in parts of southern Africa, thanks in part to new laws that give local people a share of the income elephants bring, including tourism. Barrett said these successes resulted from a clear goal with a credible plan and people who believed they could make a difference. The report calls it "the science of hope". "Hope is not the same thing as wishful thinking," he said. "Hope is not passive. Hope's about action." But despite the individual successes, the overall picture for nature remains stark. Working with the Zoological Society of London, WWF tracks nearly 36,000 populations of almost 6,000 species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians. It estimates global monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970. The figure measures the average change in the size of those populations, not the number of animals lost. About half of the populations are stable or growing, but their gains are outweighed by losses elsewhere. Dr Katie Collins, a senior curator at the Natural History Museum in London, also said the index misses out vast numbers of important species because it covers only vertebrates, missing plants, insects and other creatures they depend on. "If you lose garden snails, you lose the song thrush," she warned. WWF says conservation alone cannot reverse the decline but there must be efforts to tackle the causes. The biggest pressures come from farming, which can destroy the habitats wildlife depends on, and burning fossil fuels for energy, which drives climate change. The organisation says the money is flowing the wrong way. In 2023, about $7.3 trillion (£5.53tn) went into activities that harm nature, compared with $220bn spent protecting or restoring it, the report estimates – a ratio of roughly 33 to one. Barrett has worked on seven Living Planet reports, but he said this was the first where the takeaway message was to focus on hope. "The fact that the science is still telling us that we've got a way out is actually extraordinary," he said. "So it's a closing window of opportunity, but it's still open, just, if we act now." title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo astronauts on the moon, has died
content: Margaret Hamilton, the groundbreaking researcher who helped create the field of software engineering and whose code helped land NASA’s Apollo astronauts on the moon to win the 20th century space race, has died. She was 90. Hamilton’s former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, confirmed her death in a post from the department of aeronautics and astronautics. She died September 30, MIT reported. The cause of her death was not disclosed. It was during her time working at MIT, where she took a job in 1959 and remained until the mid-1970s, that Hamilton managed the Software Engineering Division of the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory. The division landed a contract with NASA in 1961. She ultimately led a team of 100 engineers that designed the software to guide NASA’s Apollo missions. Through her work, Hamilton is also credited as one of the founders of the field of software engineering — a term she popularized — by helping to establish it as a professional practice. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” said Olivier de Weck, the Apollo Program Professor and interim head of the MIT Department Aeronautics and Astronautics, in a statement. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” Hamilton was honored in 2016 with the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama for her contribution to science and space travel. Hamilton was born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, according to MIT, and studied at the University of Michigan before receiving her degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Indiana. She took a job at MIT while her husband studied law at Harvard. While working to develop critical onboard software for the spacecraft — both command modules and lunar landers — that completed NASA’s historic Apollo flights — Hamilton is credited with making the system more robust and accident-resistant. One oft-cited failsafe she introduced was “the Lauren error,” according to MIT, which was named for her daughter and discovered when the then-4-year-old was fiddling with an Apollo command module simulator. “She liked to play astronaut because she saw me playing that way in certain simulations we would run,” Hamilton later recalled in an oral history project. “This was in a hardware simulation because we wanted to try how the software worked with all the other things — the astronaut, the hardware. So I remember one time when Lauren’s simulation crashed and I thought, ‘Oh my god, how did that happen?’’’ So, Hamilton programmed backstops to prevent an astronaut from running into the same problem mid-flight, an issue that would have yielded far more dire consequences in space. NASA pointed to one notable example where Hamilton’s work helped ensure mission success: During the famed 1969 Apollo 11 mission, Hamilton’s software overrode an errant attempt to swap the flight computer’s primary processing to a radar system. The software’s intervention, which occurred just three minutes before the first ever touchdown on the lunar surface, “permitted the mission to safely continue,” NASA said . After its work on Apollo, the MIT Instrumentation Lab spun off to become the Charles Stark Draper Laboratory, now known as Draper Laboratory . Hamilton did not join the company, setting off instead to form her own company, but Draper’s CEO, Jerry Wohletz, said in a statement in MIT’s Wednesday announcement that Hamilton left an “indelible mark.” “Through her leadership and contributions,” Wohletz said, “she helped ensure that Apollo astronauts landed safely on the lunar surface and safely returned home. We will honor her legacy at Draper forever.” In 2003, Hamilton was also awarded NASA’s Exceptional Space Act Award. The technologist who nominated Hamilton for the honor, Paul Curto, said at the time, “I was surprised to discover she was never formally recognized for her groundbreaking work.” “Her concepts of asynchronous software, priority scheduling, end-to-end testing, and man-in-the-loop decision capability, such as priority displays, became the foundation for ultra-reliable software design,” he said.
ranking_reason: Margaret Hamilton's legacy in software engineering and her contributions to NASA's Apollo missions are significant for the scientific and technological communities.

analysis.reason: Margaret Hamilton's legacy in software engineering and her contributions to NASA's Apollo missions are significant for the scientific and technological communities.

content: An analysis of roughly 500 spear points suggests that inherited knowledge of stone deposits helped Ice Age hunters decide which tools were worth carrying. Ice Age hunters in the Tennessee River Valley sometimes threw away stone spearheads that were still usable. Leaving a point behind lightened the load, but replacing it required suitable rock, something people entering unfamiliar territory could not necessarily count on finding. “When you think about a people who are moving around a lot, understand that they didn’t have any pack animals,” said Shane Miller, an assistant professor of anthropology at the University of Alabama. “That puts limitations on what tools you discard and what you carry around. “You really don’t want to be carrying around a bag of rocks, and so you’re going to be judicious about balancing what you need versus what you can carry.” Miller and Jesse Tune, an associate professor of anthropology at the University of Mississippi and director of its Center for Archaeological Research, examined roughly 500 spear points recovered from the Tennessee River Valley. Their study, published in the Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory , compared tools left by Clovis and Cumberland groups to investigate how knowledge of local resources might have influenced what their owners kept. “How did they adapt to a place no one has ever been before?” Miller said. “We can’t interview these people, so we have to look at the things they left behind. “There aren’t that many archaeological sites for these people that we can dig, but what we have instead are lots and lots of points that people have found in this region.” Clovis groups were living in the Tennessee River Valley around 13,200 years ago , placing them among its earliest known inhabitants. Entering unfamiliar terrain meant having to locate the materials needed for daily life, including chert, a sedimentary rock well suited to making stone weapons. Skill at shaping a spearhead could only go so far without knowing where to obtain the stone. “Think about space exploration,” Tune said. “There really is no difference between Ice Age hunter-gatherers and the people sending missions and rovers to Mars. We’re moving into an area, deciding what to take with us, learning the resources, and slowly expanding. It’s the exact same process. “What we learn and how we pass on that knowledge are the same things that we’re still dealing with today. The only thing that’s changed is the technology.” Tune and Miller found that Clovis hunters were more likely to resharpen their spearheads than the later Cumberland groups. Keeping an existing point in use postponed the need to replace it, a pattern the researchers interpret as a possible way of conserving resources when hunters were less certain where to find more stone. “We hang on to stuff today, but when we’re talking about mobile hunter-gatherers, they had a different understanding and worldview when it came to personal possessions,” Tune said. “Spear points were designed to be disposable objects, and that makes what the Clovis were doing interesting.” Hunters followed seasons, rivers, and game across the Americas, carrying tools that now survive as some of the few traces of their daily lives. The researchers are using those objects to reconstruct decisions made in surroundings very different from the valley today. “We’re talking about Ice Age hunter-gatherers, people that looked and acted just like us and had the same needs that we do,” Tune said. “But they’re living in a world that is dominated by mastodons, mammoths, giant sloths – all these animals that are totally unfamiliar to us today. “What we’re looking at – the points – is a tiny part of their life, but we’re trying to see the rest of their behaviors through the lens of these spear points because that’s what we have.” Cumberland hunters followed the Clovis groups several hundred years later, leaving behind tools that gave Tune and Miller a different set of choices to examine. “When we look at the Cumberland points, we can see where they got the raw material, roughly the time period that they lived and that they’ve used the point multiple times,” Tune said. “But (the point) was rarely completely broken to the point that it couldn’t be used anymore. “So how did it end up in what was essentially the trash, and then in the archaeological record?” Cumberland hunters, the researchers suggest, inherited their predecessors’ knowledge of chert deposits and other resources. A usable spearhead left behind in the Tennessee River Valley may record the practical value of that inheritance: knowing where to find fresh stone made an old point easier to let go. Reference: “Foraging Theory and the Colonization of Unfamiliar Landscapes: Assessing Late Pleistocene Projectile Point Reduction Strategies” by Jesse W. Tune, and D. Shane Miller, 27 August 2026, Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory . DOI: 10.1007/s10816-026-09825-w Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. ranking_reason: The discovery of inherited knowledge of stone deposits among Ice Age hunters provides valuable insights into the decision-making processes of ancient societies.

analysis.reason: The discovery of inherited knowledge of stone deposits among Ice Age hunters provides valuable insights into the decision-making processes of ancient societies.
